assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength idea, which removes the light shift of the trapping field, with Ye's realization of clocks at the 10^-18 level. It is a clean case of precision atomic physics opening a new regime: clock comparisons that probe gravitational redshift at millimetre scales, tests of fundamental constants and a route to redefining the second. The idea is easy to explain and the result is robust.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early strontium clocks. Ye built the highest-performance strontium systems and pushed uncertainty and stability records. The two-name credit fits a fair prize. Other groups (PTB, NIST, JILA, SYRTE, RIKEN) made important contributions, and I would regard them as strong confirmation rather than missing co-laureates. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already covered combs and ion clocks, so this is a distinct step.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories on several continents have reproduced and improved lattice clocks over about 20 years. Performance is stable and the interpretation is not in dispute. Recognition is timely, and arguably overdue given the maturity.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a sufficiently distinct discovery after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, rather than a refinement.
Share of credit for the early lattice-clock realisation with other groups, which I have not verified in detail.
The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full impact is still pending.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators revealed a new class of electronic matter, with insulating bulk and protected conducting edges, that does not follow the symmetry-breaking paradigm. This is a fundamental discovery about how nature organizes matter, and it has influenced a whole field. It extends the 2016 topological-phase prize, which did not cover time-reversal-invariant topological insulators.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state in graphene. Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. That prediction, and the early 3D topological-insulator work of Moore, Balents, Fu and Hasan, may merit credit, but the supplied names give a workable three-person configuration. Allocation is a real difficulty, since several people made decisive contributions and I am relying on my own recollection of the history.
assessment.maturity: The HgTe edge transport was reproduced and extended, and the 3D materials were confirmed by photoemission by several groups. The theory is well established. Recognition would be timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: The exact split between theory and experiment, and whether Zhang's group (not on the credited list) is essential.
Practical applications remain limited, which does not matter for fundamental worth but may affect committee appetite.
The overlap with B002 means credit for the same discovery is expressed in two ways, and I have not weighed the quantum anomalous Hall part.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry shows matter-wave interference with whole atoms and turns it into one of the most sensitive tools for inertial and gravitational measurement. It is a direct demonstration of quantum mechanics with massive objects, and it has been used for gravity gradiometry, determinations of fundamental constants and tests of the equivalence principle. This speaks to the question of where the quantum world meets the classical.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group demonstrated early atom interferometers with gratings and later with atom-optics; Kasevich and Chu realised the light-pulse interferometer, and Mlynek's group produced the early Young double-slit and diffraction experiments with atoms. Steven Chu is not on the credited list, which weakens a clean assignment, and Chu already received the 1997 prize for cooling. I would consider Kasevich and Pritchard the strongest pair from the supplied names, but the priority story is entangled.
assessment.maturity: The field is well confirmed across many laboratories, with commercial and geodetic devices in use. Interpretation is stable. Timing is good, though some may argue part of the credit was implicitly covered by 1997 and 2001.
uncertainties: Division of credit among Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich and uncredited people such as Chu and Borde, which I cannot resolve from the packet.
Whether the discovery is judged more as a technique than a discovery.
Some claimed sensitivity gains for field applications remain more promising than demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene produced correlated insulators and unconventional superconductivity in a clean, tunable carbon system, where flat bands arise from a simple geometric twist. The result is surprising, and it launched moire quantum matter with many follow-up platforms. It is a strong case for a discovery that nobody expected a few years earlier.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle. Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated and superconducting states in 2018, and the supplied names cover this theory-plus-experiment pairing in a natural way. Others, such as Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov, made important independent contributions, and I cannot say who deserves priority.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely since 2018, but the origin of the superconductivity and the details of the correlated phases are still debated, and sample-to-sample variation is large. The theory of the single-particle flat band is mature, while the many-body physics is not yet settled. This is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity is still unsettled, so the interpretation is not stable.
Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate the experimental picture.
Credit among experimental groups is not obviously limited to one person.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase show that potentials and geometry have physical meaning in quantum mechanics, and they underlie much of modern physics, from topological matter to molecular dynamics. These are conceptual discoveries of the kind I value, ones that change how we think about the quantum world.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) predicted the effect; Bohm is deceased, so Aharonov is the eligible name, and the supplied list does not include him anyway. Berry (1984) discovered the geometric phase, with earlier related ideas from Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins. Combining two distinct discoveries into one prize is awkward. A prize to Berry and Aharonov is possible but is a compound and not wholly clean configuration.
assessment.maturity: Both effects have been verified many times, including in electron, neutron, optical and molecular systems. The age of the work is a strength for confirmation but raises the question of whether the committee has missed its moment, and of eligibility with respect to the deceased.
uncertainties: Whether the two ideas fit together in a single citation.
Priority questions around Pancharatnam, Longuet-Higgins and others, and the role of Bohm.
The Nobel committee has traditionally been wary of purely conceptual advances without a decisive single experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos, later linked to the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the active galaxy NGC 1068, opened a new window on the high-energy universe. It is an experimental discovery of something new, achieved with an unusual detector in the Antarctic ice. I defer to colleagues on astroparticle physics, but the importance is evident.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the IceCube concept and its predecessor AMANDA; Karle and Spiering made key contributions to detector development and the discovery analysis. The collaboration is large, which complicates credit, but the supplied names offer a reasonable three-person configuration. I cannot independently judge the relative weights.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is established at high significance, and source identification is progressing, with the 2018 and 2022 results. Independent confirmation by other experiments such as Baikal-GVD and KM3NeT is still limited, and source populations are not fully understood. The timing is reasonable but perhaps a little early for the source-identification part.
uncertainties: Independent confirmation by other detectors is still limited.
Most astrophysical sources are not identified, so the interpretation is incomplete.
Relative contributions of Halzen, Karle and Spiering versus other leaders and the collaboration, which I cannot verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade lets individual neutral atoms interact strongly and controllably, which allows programmable arrays of tweezers-trapped atoms to be used for quantum simulation and gate operations. This is atomic physics I know well, with a natural link to precise control of quantum states and many-body dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and collaborators developed the blockade-based gate proposals, Browaeys's group made early demonstrations of blockade between single atoms and quantum simulation with arrays, and Lukin's group has driven large programmable arrays and many-body experiments. The list omits others who demonstrated blockade first, such as Grangier and Gould and their groups, and I cannot be sure about their ranking.
assessment.maturity: The approach is reproduced by several groups and is developing rapidly, with error-corrected logical operations emerging. The pace is good for science but the field is still evolving, so recognition may be a little premature.
uncertainties: Priority for the first blockade observations between single atoms is uncertain.
Whether the long-term significance will be the discovery or a technology platform, which is not yet clear.
Scalability and fault tolerance claims are still being tested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Proposals and experiments for quantum information processing with trapped ions and neutral atoms showed how controlled quantum systems can be engineered for computation and simulation. The Cirac-Zoller gate proposal was a conceptual step, and Blatt's experiments gave early demonstrations of entanglement and gates with ions. The work is important and clearly foundational for the field.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the ion-trap quantum computer in 1995 and the idea of atom-based quantum simulation; Blatt realised many of the first gates and algorithms in ions. Bloch is also credited but the three-name set looks most natural for the ion-based part. Wineland's 2012 prize and the 2022 entanglement prize already cover related ground, so the margin for a new prize is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is extensive and the interpretation is stable. The concept is mature, though it is arguably partially covered by earlier prizes, which affects the case for recognition now.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 and 2022 prizes lowers the case for a new award.
Whether the proposals or the experimental realisations should be given weight.
Whether the committee wants to split theory and experiment differently, for example bringing in Bloch and neutral-atom simulation.
